questions.q: How does this lesson relate the Lightning Page vs. LWC decision to Lesson 17's Flow vs. Apex reasoning?
options: They are entirely unrelated decisions with no shared logic
LWC development is always required regardless of what Lightning App Builder can provide

It's the same underlying trade-off applied to UI: assembling existing components declaratively in App Builder is generally cheaper to build and maintain, and custom LWC development should be reserved for needs standard composition genuinely can't meet
Lightning App Builder and LWC are mutually exclusive and can never be used on the same page
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames this as the UI-design equivalent of the declarative-vs-programmatic reasoning: check what App Builder's declarative composition can achieve before reaching for custom LWC development.

questions.q: Which of these is given in this lesson as a case where a custom LWC is justified?
options: A highly specific interactive visualization or multi-step guided interaction that doesn't match any standard component's behavior
Replicating exactly what a standard related list already does, with a marginally different look
Displaying a single plain text field on a record page
Any situation where a developer happens to be available
questions.explain: The lesson specifically names highly specific interactions, custom visualizations, and components meant for wide reuse as justified custom-LWC cases, while warning against building custom just to replicate existing standard functionality.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the LWC-vs-declarative-assembly decision doesn't need to be made once for an entire application?
options: Because only one UI technology can ever be used per Salesforce org
Because Lightning App Builder cannot display any custom components at all
Because this decision is made exclusively by Salesforce support, not the architect

Because Lightning web components and the older Aura model can run side by side on the same page, so different pieces of the same page can mix standard components and custom LWCs, each chosen on its own merits
questions.explain: Since components (LWC and Aura) coexist on the same page transparently to the admin assembling it, each piece of a page can be decided on its own merits rather than forcing one global choice for the whole application.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why is mobile-first design described as a constraint at design time rather than a later responsive fix?
options: Because mobile usage is negligible and not worth considering

Because a UI designed and tested only on desktop can be genuinely unusable on a real phone screen, and retrofitting mobile consideration later is markedly more expensive than designing for it from the start
Because Salesforce's mobile app renders every desktop layout identically with no issues
Because mobile-first design only applies to Experience Cloud sites, never internal apps
questions.explain: The lesson argues that content prioritization for small screens is a design decision, not something Lightning's responsive behavior automatically fixes, and that retrofitting this after the fact costs more than designing for it from the start.

questions.q: What does this lesson identify as the real failure in cramming a full desktop layout onto a mobile screen?
options: It's purely a rendering bug that Salesforce will eventually patch automatically
It never causes any real usability issues in practice
It's actually a content-prioritization problem -- deciding what fields and actions matter most on a small screen -- not just a rendering problem
It only affects Lightning Web Components, never standard components
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly distinguishes the content-prioritization problem (what actually matters on a phone screen) from a pure rendering issue, arguing the former is what mobile-first design at design time is meant to address.
